questions.stem: The Iceni, Boudicca's people, lived in the area of modern:
options: Wales and the island of Anglesey
Yorkshire and the Pennine hills in the north
Norfolk and north Suffolk in East Anglia
Kent and Sussex on the south-east coast
questions.explanation: The Iceni territory was in East Anglia, roughly modern Norfolk and parts of Suffolk. Anglesey (Mona) was where the governor Suetonius Paulinus was campaigning when the revolt began, and the Brigantes held much of the north.

questions.stem: Before the Roman conquest, Britain was best described as:
options: an empty frontier settled only after the Romans arrived
a land of separate tribes, each with its own rulers
a single kingdom ruled by a high king from Camulodunum
a group of Greek trading colonies set along the southern coast
questions.explanation: Iron Age Britain was divided among many tribes, such as the Iceni, Trinovantes, Catuvellauni and Brigantes, who were often rivals. No single king ruled the whole island, which helped Rome conquer it piece by piece.

questions.stem: Gold torcs such as those found in hoards at Snettisham in Norfolk are evidence that the Iceni region before the conquest:
options: had a wealthy elite and skilled metalworkers
was too poor to produce any fine metalwork
imported all its jewellery from Roman Italy
had no leaders or differences in social rank
questions.explanation: The Snettisham hoards contain many fine gold and silver torcs made by local craftsmen, showing wealth and status display in the area. They pre-date the Roman conquest, so they are not Roman imports.

questions.stem: Iceni coins found by archaeologists are useful to historians mainly because they:
options: record the date of Boudicca's birth and the names of her two daughters
prove the Iceni used Latin as their everyday spoken language
show that the Iceni paid all their taxes to Rome in gold coin
show that the tribe had rulers and how far its influence spread
questions.explanation: Tribal coins, some carrying abbreviated names of rulers, and their find spots help map Iceni territory and authority. They do not record personal details such as Boudicca's family, and Celtic Britons did not speak Latin as their everyday language.

questions.stem: The Roman conquest of Britain began in 43 CE under the emperor:
options: Augustus
Nero
Vespasian
Claudius
questions.explanation: Claudius launched the invasion in 43 CE under the general Aulus Plautius and came to Britain for the capture of Camulodunum. Nero was emperor at the time of Boudicca's revolt.

questions.stem: After 43 CE some British tribes, including the Iceni under Prasutagus, kept their own kings as allies of Rome. Such rulers are known as:
options: proconsuls
tribunes of the plebs
Druid high priests
client kings
questions.explanation: Client kings kept their thrones in return for loyalty to Rome, which saved Rome the cost of direct rule. Proconsuls governed senatorial provinces, and British Iceni rulers were not Roman officials.

questions.stem: In 47 CE the governor Ostorius Scapula ordered British tribes to be disarmed. According to Tacitus, how did the Iceni respond?
options: They asked Claudius to make them Roman citizens
They rose in revolt and were defeated
They handed over their weapons without protest
They fled across the sea to Gaul
questions.explanation: Tacitus records that the Iceni resisted the disarming and were defeated. This earlier revolt shows that tension between the Iceni and Rome existed well before Boudicca.

questions.stem: In Roman Britain, the governor and the procurator had different roles. Which statement is correct?
options: The governor led the army; the procurator managed imperial finances
The governor collected taxes; the procurator commanded the legions in the field
Both were elected each year by the Britons of the province
The procurator was the chief priest of the imperial cult at Londinium
questions.explanation: The governor (an imperial legate) held military and judicial power, while the procurator answered directly to the emperor for finances. In 60/61 CE these were Suetonius Paulinus and Catus Decianus.

questions.stem: Camulodunum (Colchester) became a colonia for retired soldiers about 49 CE. Tacitus says the veterans angered the Trinovantes because they:
options: refused to farm and lived only on food sent from Italy
forced the Trinovantes to fight in the legions overseas
banned all trade between the colony and the surrounding native Britons
drove locals from their homes and treated them like captives
questions.explanation: Tacitus describes the veterans taking land and homes and calling the Britons captives and slaves, with soldiers backing them. This grievance explains why the Trinovantes joined the Iceni.

questions.stem: The temple of the deified Claudius at Camulodunum was resented by the Britons mainly because:
options: it housed the Ninth Legion, which guarded the colony
it stood for Roman rule, and the chosen priests had to pay for its cult
it was dedicated to a British god whom the Roman soldiers had openly insulted
it was built on the site of the Iceni royal palace
questions.explanation: Tacitus calls the temple a citadel of everlasting domination, and says the Britons chosen as its priests spent their fortunes on the cult. It was part of the imperial cult, which honoured the deified emperor.

questions.stem: Which two ancient writers give the main written accounts of Boudicca's revolt?
options: Livy and Polybius
Suetonius and Plutarch
Tacitus and Cassius Dio
Julius Caesar and Strabo
questions.explanation: Tacitus describes the revolt in the Agricola and the Annals, and Cassius Dio in his Roman History. Caesar wrote about Britain a century earlier, and the biographer Suetonius does not narrate the revolt in detail.

questions.stem: Why do many historians regard Tacitus as a well-informed source on the revolt?
options: He copied his account directly from an Iceni written chronicle
His father-in-law Agricola served under Paulinus in Britain at the time
He was born in Londinium and saw the city burned as a young boy
He interviewed Boudicca's daughters, who lived in Rome after the revolt
questions.explanation: Gnaeus Julius Agricola, whose daughter Tacitus married, was a young officer on Paulinus's staff, so Tacitus may have had eyewitness information. Tacitus himself was not in Britain in 60/61 CE, and the Iceni left no written histories.

questions.stem: Cassius Dio wrote in Greek in the early third century CE, and his account of the revolt survives mainly in a later Byzantine summary. What is the main problem this creates?
options: His account contradicts every fact recorded by archaeology
He never mentions Boudicca by name in any surviving passage
He wrote long after the event, and we may not have his exact words
He was a Briton himself, so he exaggerated the success of the Iceni
questions.explanation: Dio wrote about 150 years after the revolt, and his work for these years survives largely in an epitome made by a later Byzantine writer, so details may have been lost or changed. He was a Roman senator from Bithynia, not a Briton.

questions.stem: Cassius Dio gives a detailed description of Boudicca's appearance: very tall, with a harsh voice, a mass of tawny hair and a great golden torc. How should a historian treat this description?
options: As proof that Boudicca wore Roman dress to win over the province
As a description written by Boudicca's daughters for a Roman audience
As a literary portrait of a fearsome barbarian, not an eyewitness record
As an accurate likeness copied from an official Roman portrait statue of her
questions.explanation: Dio wrote long after the revolt and was shaping a dramatic image of a terrifying barbarian woman. Some details, such as the torc, fit Celtic culture, but no contemporary portrait of Boudicca exists.

questions.stem: Tacitus and Dio both give Boudicca long speeches before battle. A historian should use these speeches mainly as evidence of:
options: the battle plan agreed by the British chiefs
Roman views of tyranny, freedom and barbarian women
Boudicca's exact words, taken down by Roman army scribes
the Celtic language spoken by the Iceni
questions.explanation: Ancient historians composed speeches for their characters to convey themes. Tacitus uses Boudicca to criticise Roman greed and abuse, so the speeches reveal Roman ideas rather than the queen's words.

questions.stem: Excavations in Colchester and London have found a layer of burnt debris, including burnt daub and charred goods, dated to about 60/61 CE. This evidence:
options: supports the written accounts that the towns were burned
proves that the fires were started by the Roman army
shows that both towns were abandoned forever afterwards
gives the exact number of people killed in each town
questions.explanation: The destruction horizon in Camulodunum and Londinium matches Tacitus and Dio on the burning of the towns. Both towns were rebuilt, and burnt layers cannot show casualty numbers.

questions.stem: In 2014 a hoard of gold jewellery and coins, the Fenwick Treasure, was found buried beneath the floor of a house in Colchester. What is the most reasonable inference?
options: A resident hid valuables during the revolt and never recovered them
The Iceni buried their royal treasure in Camulodunum before the conquest
The Romans paid the Iceni a large tribute in gold after the revolt
Boudicca's own jewellery was buried at the site of her death
questions.explanation: The hoard was buried in a house within the destruction layer, suggesting a Roman-era resident hid it as the rebels approached. The owner's failure to recover it hints at their fate, but it is not linked to Boudicca herself.

questions.stem: A bronze head of Claudius, broken from a statue, was found in the River Alde in Suffolk in 1907. Many historians link it to the revolt because:
options: it was cast by Iceni craftsmen to honour Prasutagus as a client king
it carries an inscription naming Boudicca as the one who broke it
it was buried with Suetonius Paulinus after his death in Britain
it may have been looted from Camulodunum by the rebels and later dumped
questions.explanation: The head appears to have been hacked from a statue and carried far from any Roman town, which fits rebels sacking Camulodunum. There is no inscription linking it to Boudicca, so the connection is an inference.

questions.stem: Prasutagus, king of the Iceni and Boudicca's husband, left his kingdom in his will to:
options: the Roman governor Suetonius Paulinus
the emperor Nero and his own two daughters
his wife Boudicca alone, as sole queen
the Trinovantes, his closest allies
questions.explanation: Tacitus says Prasutagus made the emperor co-heir with his two daughters, hoping to protect his kingdom and family. Rome ignored the will and treated the kingdom as conquered territory.

questions.stem: According to Tacitus, after Prasutagus died Roman officials:
options: made Boudicca a Roman citizen and gave her new lands
kept the kingdom independent until her daughters came of age
invited Boudicca to Rome to meet the emperor Nero
flogged Boudicca, raped her daughters and seized Iceni estates
questions.explanation: Tacitus records that the kingdom was plundered, Boudicca was flogged, her daughters were raped and the leading Iceni were stripped of their estates. These outrages are the immediate trigger of the revolt in his account.

questions.stem: Cassius Dio adds a financial cause of the revolt that Tacitus does not stress. What was it?
options: The procurator ordered all British gold to be melted down for coins
Rome doubled the grain tax after a run of poor harvests
Loans pressed on the Britons were recalled and earlier gifts demanded back
Nero banned the Britons from trading with Gaul, ruining their merchants and farmers
questions.explanation: Dio says the procurator Catus Decianus reclaimed money Claudius had given to leading Britons, and that Seneca called in large loans. Tacitus focuses more on the treatment of the Iceni royal family and the colony at Camulodunum.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why the revolt spread beyond the Iceni?
options: The Romans had executed the kings of every tribe in southern Britain
The Druids ordered all Britons to join the Iceni on pain of death
Other tribes, such as the Trinovantes, had grievances of their own
Boudicca was already the elected war leader of all the tribes of Britain
questions.explanation: Tacitus says the Trinovantes and others joined because of the colony at Camulodunum, the temple of Claudius and Roman greed. The revolt drew on wider resentment, not a single command structure.

questions.stem: When the revolt broke out, the governor Suetonius Paulinus was campaigning on Mona (Anglesey) against:
options: Caledonian tribes in the far north of Scotland
pirates raiding the coast of Gaul
the Druids and the Britons who sheltered there
the Brigantes and their queen Cartimandua
questions.explanation: Mona was a centre of the Druids and a refuge for opponents of Rome, and Paulinus attacked it in 60/61 CE. His absence in the far west gave the rebels time to attack the undefended south-east.

questions.stem: Which town did the rebels attack and destroy first?
options: Isca (Exeter)
Camulodunum (Colchester)
Londinium (London)
Verulamium (St Albans)
questions.explanation: The rebels first stormed Camulodunum, where the last defenders held out in the temple of Claudius for two days. Londinium and Verulamium were destroyed afterwards.

questions.stem: Part of the Ninth Legion under Petillius Cerialis marched to relieve Camulodunum. What happened?
options: It defeated Boudicca's army and captured her daughters
Its infantry was cut down, and Cerialis escaped with his cavalry
It reached the colony in time and saved the temple of Claudius
It joined the rebels after its commander was killed
questions.explanation: Tacitus says the rebels routed the Ninth Legion's force and slaughtered its infantry, while Cerialis fled to his camp with the cavalry. This success encouraged the revolt to spread.

questions.stem: Suetonius Paulinus reached Londinium ahead of the rebels but decided to leave it. Why?
options: He wanted to join the Second Legion waiting at Camulodunum
He judged his force too small to hold it and chose to save the province
He was ordered by Nero to retreat to Gaul at once
Londinium had already been burned to the ground by the time his army arrived
questions.explanation: Tacitus says Paulinus decided to sacrifice one town to save the province as a whole, taking with him those who could keep up. Camulodunum had already fallen, so it was not a place to retreat to.

questions.stem: Tacitus says about 70,000 Roman citizens and allies were killed in the three towns, while Dio gives 80,000. How should a historian treat these figures?
options: As figures confirmed by counting skeletons in the burnt layers
As the ancient writers' claims, probably rounded and unverifiable
As exact counts taken from official Roman census records
As proof that the towns held more people than Rome itself
questions.explanation: Ancient writers often gave large round numbers, and neither writer could have had an accurate count. Archaeology confirms the destruction but has found relatively few bodies, so the figures cannot be checked.

questions.stem: Poenius Postumus, camp prefect of the Second Legion, refused Paulinus's order to bring his troops. What did he do after the Roman victory?
options: He was made governor of Britain in reward
He fled to the Iceni and joined the survivors
He led the punitive campaign against the Trinovantes
He killed himself by falling on his sword
questions.explanation: Tacitus says Postumus, having denied his legion a share in the victory, fell on his sword. His refusal meant Paulinus fought with a much smaller army than he might have.

questions.stem: Tacitus says Paulinus chose to fight in a narrow defile with woods behind him and open ground in front. Why was this a good choice?
options: It hid his army so that the Britons could not find it for several weeks
It let his chariots charge downhill into the British infantry
It placed a river between the two armies so no battle could begin
It stopped the larger British army surrounding his outnumbered troops
questions.explanation: The narrow position protected the Roman flanks and rear and forced the Britons to attack on a narrow front, where Roman discipline counted most. The Britons, not the Romans, used chariots.

questions.stem: Which feature of Celtic warfare is described by the ancient sources on the final battle?
options: Chariots and a mass charge, with families watching from wagons
Ranks of armoured pikemen in a tight phalanx eight rows deep
Mounted archers firing from horseback while circling the enemy
War elephants used to break the line of Roman infantry
questions.explanation: Tacitus describes Boudicca driving a chariot with her daughters, a huge mass of warriors and wagons carrying families at the edge of the field. Phalanxes, horse archers and elephants belong to other armies.

questions.stem: Tacitus says the legionaries threw their javelins and then advanced in a wedge formation. Why was this effective against the British attack?
options: The wedge formation allowed the Romans to surround the Britons from the start
Pila broke the charge, then close-order troops fought with short swords
The wedge let the Romans retreat quickly into their fortified camp
The javelins were set on fire to frighten the British horses
questions.explanation: The pilum disrupted an attacking mass and could disable shields, and disciplined troops with large shields and the short gladius then fought at close quarters. Long Celtic slashing swords needed space that the press of battle denied.

questions.stem: Tacitus claims almost 80,000 Britons died in the final battle for the loss of about 400 Romans. Which factor in his own account best explains a one-sided defeat?
options: The battle was fought at night, when the Britons could not see
The Britons' own wagons at the rear blocked their escape when they broke
The Britons ran out of arrows before the Romans reached them
Boudicca's army included Roman deserters who changed sides mid-battle
questions.explanation: Tacitus says the ring of wagons hemmed in the fleeing Britons, so they were slaughtered. His exact figures are doubtful, but the trapping of a routed army explains a heavy defeat.

questions.stem: The site of the final battle between Boudicca and Paulinus is:
options: unknown, though many places in the Midlands are suggested
marked by a Roman victory monument just outside the walls of Londinium
the island of Mona, where the Druids were defeated
Camulodunum, within the walls of the burnt colony
questions.explanation: Tacitus gives a description of the ground but no place name, so its location is debated, with sites along the Roman road later called Watling Street often proposed. No battlefield has been confirmed by archaeology.

questions.stem: How do Tacitus and Dio differ on Boudicca's death?
options: Tacitus says she took poison; Dio says she fell ill and died
Tacitus says she was killed in battle; Dio says she escaped to Gaul
Tacitus says she was taken to Rome; Dio says she was executed in Britain
Both say she was captured, but differ on how she was executed
questions.explanation: Tacitus says Boudicca ended her life with poison, while Dio says she fell sick and died and was given a costly burial. Neither says she was captured or paraded in Rome.

questions.stem: Which was a consequence of the revolt for the Britons who had taken part?
options: Full Roman citizenship granted to all the tribes of southern Britain
The return of the Iceni kingdom to Boudicca's daughters
The removal of all Roman troops from East Anglia
Punitive campaigns and famine, since many had not sown their crops
questions.explanation: Tacitus describes Roman forces ravaging hostile territory and famine among tribes who had counted on seizing Roman supplies instead of planting. The Iceni kingdom was not restored.

questions.stem: The new procurator, Julius Classicianus, reported to Rome that Paulinus's harsh reprisals would prevent peace, and Paulinus was soon replaced by Petronius Turpilianus. What does this suggest about Roman policy after the revolt?
options: Rome rewarded Paulinus for crushing the revolt with a second term
Rome handed control of Britain to the client queen Cartimandua
Rome moved towards conciliation to restore order and revenue
Rome decided to abandon Britain and withdraw all its legions
questions.explanation: Tacitus says Nero sent his freedman Polyclitus to investigate, and Paulinus was recalled soon after. The milder governors who followed suggest Rome wanted a settled, tax-paying province. Classicianus's tombstone survives from London.

questions.stem: Thomas Thornycroft's bronze statue of Boudicca in a chariot with her daughters stands near Westminster Bridge in London. It mainly reflects:
options: Roman official art celebrating Paulinus's great victory over the Iceni
an exact likeness based on coins issued by Boudicca herself
a modern Welsh campaign to return her remains to Anglesey
nineteenth-century British pride, which made her a national symbol
questions.explanation: Victorian Britain saw Boudicca as a patriotic heroine, often linked with Queen Victoria, whose name also suggests victory. The statue was erected in 1902 and tells us about that era rather than the first century CE.

questions.stem: Boudicca has been represented as a freedom fighter, a savage barbarian and a feminist icon. What best explains these different representations?
options: New archaeological finds have revealed her diary and letters
The ancient sources agree in every detail, so only the art differs
Each version comes from a different eyewitness to the revolt
Each age has used her story to suit its own values and purposes
questions.explanation: Because the sources are few and written by Romans, later writers and artists have shaped Boudicca to fit national pride, ideas about women or anti-imperial views. No writings by Boudicca survive.
